edges.description: Alternative splicing directs neurogenesis, cortical lamination and synaptogenesis, and the patients have malformations of cortical development; but no study has connected NSRP1 to any of those steps. This edge records that the disease runs from the splicing defect to the brain without recording how.

edges.description: Reduced head circumference accompanies the cortical malformation in five of six patients, over a wide range of severity.
The gyral simplification is itself the malformation this node names.
Failure of the frontal and temporal opercula to close over the insula, a developmental rather than acquired appearance.
Superior and/or inferior vermian hypoplasia in three of four imaged patients.
Callosal dysgenesis in one of four imaged patients.
A thin brainstem in one of four imaged patients.

Attributing the spastic quadriparesis to the malformations is the standard clinical reading of a static encephalopathy with abnormal imaging, and it is what makes NSRP1 a candidate cerebral palsy gene. No study in this disease tests it, and the imaged malformations are not confined to motor pathways, so the step is recorded as unestablished.

Epilepsy in a malformed cortex is the expected pairing, and every patient had both. Nothing in this disease shows the malformations generate the seizures, and no electrophysiological study of NSRP1 loss exists.
Developmental delay was present in all six patients of the founding cohort and in the 2024 case, alongside the malformation.
Appendicular spasticity in all six patients of the founding cohort.
Hypotonia in all six, coexisting with the limb spasticity rather than replacing it.
The quadriparetic distribution the authors name.
A static spastic motor impairment of developmental origin is what cerebral palsy describes, and the authors propose NSRP1 as a cerebral palsy gene on exactly that basis.
Three of six patients were non-ambulatory.
Five of six were non-verbal. Whether this follows the motor impairment, the cognitive one, or both is not addressed.
Dysphagia in four of six, a bulbar counterpart of the motor impairment.
Epilepsy in all six patients of the founding cohort.
Abnormal electroencephalography in all patients, with epileptiform discharges the commonest finding.

Complete loss of the mouse gene is lethal shortly after implantation, so the model cannot show the human phenotype at all. It is included because that failure is informative: it is the main reason the authors suspect the human alleles are hypomorphic rather than null.
edges.limitations: The animal dies before the brain exists, so no neurodevelopmental, motor or electrographic phenotype can be observed. It is also a complete null, where every reported human allele retains some function or some transcript, so it does not model any patient genotype.
edges.target: Loss of NSRP1-Dependent Alternative Splice Site Selection

edges.description: The model removes NSRP1 from one lineage and measures what happens to splicing genome-wide. That measurement is the only direct evidence that losing NSRP1 shifts isoform ratios of other splicing factors and of cell-cycle transcripts.
edges.limitations: The deleted lineage is the T cell, which the human disease does not involve; no patient has reported immunodeficiency. Whether the transcripts identified here are the ones that matter in a neural progenitor is untested, so the model grounds the existence of the splicing consequence and not its identity in the brain.

nodes.description: Five variant alleles across four families: two final-exon frameshifts (c.1359_1362delAAAG, p.Glu455AlafsTer20; c.1272dupG, p.Lys425GlufsTer5), an exon 2 nonsense allele (c.52C>T, p.Gln18Ter), a canonical splice-donor allele (c.114+2T>G) and a missense allele inside the nuclear localization signal (c.1595T>A, p.Val532Glu). The three homozygous alleles were found in families from Egypt, Iran and Pakistan; the splice-donor and missense alleles were compound heterozygous in the 2024 case. The alleles split by molecular route rather than by severity alone: the two frameshifts and the missense allele act on the nuclear localization signal, while the nonsense and splice-donor alleles deplete transcript.

nodes.description: The nematode ortholog of NSRP1 is ccdc-55. Animals homozygous for the probable null allele arrest in early larval development, which is the invertebrate counterpart of the mouse lethality. RNAi depletion is milder and lets development proceed, and in that background the distal tip cell fails to stop migrating at the end of larval morphogenesis. That graded severity, lethal null against viable partial loss, is the model system's contribution to the argument that the human alleles are hypomorphic.

nodes.description: NSRP1 normally sits in nuclear speckles, the subnuclear compartment holding the splicing machinery, where it colocalizes and physically interacts with SC35 (SRSF2) and ASF/SF2 (SRSF1). The 2024 case supplies the direct observation for one patient allele; for the two frameshift alleles the step rests on the earlier deletion work rather than on patient material.

nodes.description: NSRP1 selects alternative splice sites on target pre-mRNA, shown with CD44, Tra2β1 and Fas minigene reporters, and its first RS-like subregion is required both for binding target RNA and for the splicing effect. The molecular function bound here is NSRP1's engagement of target pre-mRNA; no study has measured that binding in patient cells, so the decrease is inferred from the protein's exclusion from the nucleus rather than observed.

nodes.description: Deleting Nsrp1 in the T-cell lineage escapes the embryonic lethality and gives the only global splicing readout of NSRP1 loss in any tissue. Loss of NSrp70 changed the alternative processing of several RNA splicing factors, SRSF1 among them, and the thymocytes failed to mature, with insufficient T-cell receptor signalling and uncontrolled growth and death; the mice were severely lymphopenic. nodes.description: A gene-trap allele of mouse Nsrp1. No homozygous animal was recovered among more than 95 offspring of heterozygous intercrosses, and no homozygous embryo was found between embryonic days 6.5 and 19.5, placing the lethality shortly after implantation. Heterozygotes were indistinguishable from wild-type in body weight, protein level, interleukin-2 response and T-cell migration. The model is the strongest evidence that the gene is essential, and it is also why nobody has been able to study NSRP1 in a mouse brain.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities included under-opercularization (3/4), simplified gyral pattern (3/4), superior and/or inferior cerebellar vermian hypoplasia (3/4), corpus callosum dysgenesis (1/4), and thin brainstem (1/4)

nodes.description: NSRP1 binds SRSF1 and SRSF2 through its RS-like region and reverses their effect on splice-site choice, and its first RS-like subregion is also needed to keep both NSRP1 and the SR proteins positioned in speckles. Without NSRP1 that opposition is absent. How much this contributes is genuinely unsettled: the 2011 study found no change in SR-protein splicing activity when it knocked NSrp70 down, where the 2016 study, using deletion constructs, reports the opposition. Both results are recorded, and the disagreement is carried as a discussion.
nodes.id: Unopposed SRSF1 and SRSF2 Splicing Activity

biological_processes: SRSF1- and SRSF2-driven alternative splice site selection

evidence.reference_title: Nuclear Speckle-related Protein 70 Binds to Serine/Arginine-rich Splicing Factors 1 and 2 via an Arginine/Serine-like Region and Counteracts Their Alternative Splicing Activity.
evidence.snippet: we demonstrated that NSrp70 interacts physically with two SR proteins, SRSF1 and SRSF2, and reverses their splicing activity in terms of CD44 exon v5 as exon exclusion

evidence.reference_title: Nuclear Speckle-related Protein 70 Binds to Serine/Arginine-rich Splicing Factors 1 and 2 via an Arginine/Serine-like Region and Counteracts Their Alternative Splicing Activity.
evidence.snippet: RS1 deletion also resulted in the loss of NSrp70 and SR protein speckle positioning, implying a potential scaffolding role for NSrp70 in nuclear speckles

evidence.reference_title: NSrp70 is a novel nuclear speckle-related protein that modulates alternative pre-mRNA splicing in vivo.
evidence.snippet: we did not see any difference in terms of alternative splicing activity and speckle localization when NSrp70 expression was down-regulated by siRNA

nodes.description: Compound heterozygous with c.1595T>A in the 2024 case. A canonical splice-donor variant. No transcript study of it is reported.

evidence.reference_title: A milder form of NSRP1-associated neurodevelopmental disorder, caused by a missense variant in the nuclear localization signal.
evidence.snippet: Whole-genome sequencing revealed the compound heterozygous NSRP1 variants c.114 + 2T > G and c.1595T > A (p.Val532Glu)

nodes.description: Homozygous in Family 2, from Iran. A final-exon frameshift in a 13-base polypurine stretch, with the same predicted consequence as the Family 1 allele. It is the only one of the three founding alleles present in gnomAD, as a single heterozygote.

evidence.reference_title: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in the splicing regulator NSRP1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with spastic cerebral palsy and epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: Molecular analysis identified three pathogenic NSRP1 predicted loss-of-function variant alleles: c.1359_1362delAAAG (p.Glu455AlafsTer20), c.1272dupG (p.Lys425GlufsTer5), and c.52C>T (p.Gln18Ter)

nodes.description: Homozygous in Family 1, from Egypt. A final-exon frameshift: the transcript is predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay, so the consequence is a protein lacking the C-terminal nuclear localization signal rather than an absent protein.

evidence.reference_title: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in the splicing regulator NSRP1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with spastic cerebral palsy and epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: Molecular analysis identified three pathogenic NSRP1 predicted loss-of-function variant alleles: c.1359_1362delAAAG (p.Glu455AlafsTer20), c.1272dupG (p.Lys425GlufsTer5), and c.52C>T (p.Gln18Ter)

nodes.description: Compound heterozygous with c.114+2T>G in the 2024 case. A missense substitution inside the nuclear localization signal, and the only patient allele whose effect on localization has been measured rather than predicted: GFP-tagged mutant protein mislocalized to the cytosol in transfected HEK293T cells. The patient is the mildest reported, walking unassisted and speaking in short sentences.

evidence.reference_title: A milder form of NSRP1-associated neurodevelopmental disorder, caused by a missense variant in the nuclear localization signal.
evidence.snippet: Functional validation using HEK293T cells transfected with either wild-type or mutated GFP-tagged Nsrp1 suggests that the Val532Glu variant interferes with the function of the nuclear localization signal, and leads to mislocalization of NSRP1 in the cytosol

nodes.description: Homozygous in Family 3, from Pakistan. An exon 2 nonsense allele whose transcript is predicted to be degraded. Two things set it apart: the position is non-coding in a major alternative NSRP1 transcript, so the allele may not remove all NSRP1 protein, and this family is the mildest of the three, with less severe epilepsy and more milestones achieved.
